# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–24 (Complete – Updated 173)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of sixth year** (Chapter 24). Duel between Rawdon and Steyne occurred; outcome resolved without public scandal. Rawdon accepted Coventry Island Governorship (three thousand a year). Little Rawdon remains at school. Amelia continues living at Russell Square area, overseeing Georgy's education and relationship with his grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opened "autumn of sixth year"; Chapter 24 opens "winter of sixth year."
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens); Coventry Island (where Rawdon now Governor); Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe hill farms; Bryngate market town; Madras (India); St. Helena; Cape; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Southampton.

## The Duel Resolution and Its Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23–24)

**Macmurdo's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: When Rawdon wavered after learning of Coventry Island appointment, Macmurdo rebuked him, insisting affair was placed in his hands. Refused to carry further challenge; argued duel would disgrace all parties. Advised Rawdon to accept Coventry Island position and maintain silence.

**Duel Occurred (Chapter 24)**: Secret rencontre occurred between Rawdon and Steyne; principals and seconds agreed to bury outcome "in the profoundest oblivion." Despite sworn secrecy, story spread rapidly across London within hours. **Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Mr. Wagg acting on Wenham's hint**—duel remained town-talk for three days but kept from press.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation (Chapter 24)**: Rawdon refused Pitt's attempt to convey reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money from him ten years; she swore she had none from Steyne, but "directly I found it" she knew "it was all up." Rawdon declared: "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty, and I'll never see her again--never."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship (Chapter 24)**: Initially resisted appointment "procured for him by so odious a patron" (Steyne). Persuaded to accept by Pitt's entreaties and mainly Macmurdo's argument that Steyne would be "in a fury" if enemy's fortune was made through his means—accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Final Dissolution (Chapter 24)

**Household Seized**: Bailiffs and brokers seized Raggles's property in Curzon Street. Rebecca's fate immediately after unknown—"where? Who cared!"

**Rumors and Speculation**: World divided on guilt; rumors proliferated across European locations (Naples, Palermo, Bierstadt, Boulogne, Cheltenham).

**Financial Arrangements**: Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity"—she possessed talent for "making a little money go a great way."

## Rawdon's Life in Coventry Island (Chapter 24)

**Colonial Governance**: Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand a year. Sent Macmurdo cigars; sent Lady Jane colonial produce. Sent brother Swamp Town Gazette. Little Rawdon enjoyed reading papers about his Excellency.

**Obligations Maintained**: Remitted to Pitt punctually; wrote to little Rawdon regularly every mail. Cannot obtain life insurance (island climate too dangerous) to pay debts on leaving England.

**Moral Regeneration**: Complete transformation accomplished. Maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education and future, compensates those wronged (Briggs via Pitt), and accepts prosperity gained through enemy's patronage as ironic justice and quiet revenge.

## Georgy Osborne's Establishment and Education (Chapter 24)

**Current Status and Household**: Georgy "fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square, occupant of his father's room in the house and heir apparent of all the splendours there." Mr. Osborne (grandfather) "as proud of him as ever he had been of the elder George"—boy's "good looks, gallant bearing, and gentlemanlike appearance" won grandsire's heart.

**Intellectual Superiority**: Georgy's previous education under Amelia made him "a much better gentleman" than his grandfather's plans. Georgy's "quick brain and better education" showed boy grandfather was "a dullard." Boy began "accordingly to command him and to look down upon him."

**Physical Appearance and Dress**: Scarcely eleven years old; wore straps and beautiful little boots "like a man," gilt spurs, gold-headed whip, fine pin in handkerchief, neatest kid gloves. Famous tailor Mr. Woolsey of Conduit Street created fancy trousers, waistcoats, jackets, white waistcoats for evening parties, cut velvet waistcoats for dinners, "dear little darling shawl dressing-gown." Dressed for dinner every day "like a regular West End swell." One domestic specially attended him.

**Daily Habits and Character**: After breakfast, sat in arm-chair in dining-room reading Morning Post "just like a grown-up man." Servants delighted: "How he DU dam and swear." Those remembering Captain his father "declared Master George was his Pa, every inch of him." Made house lively "by his activity, his imperiousness, his scolding, and his good-nature." Domineer[s] "over everybody with whom he came in contact"; "in Russell Square, everybody was afraid of Mr. Osborne, and Mr. Osborne was afraid of Georgy."

**Friendships and Entertainments**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Master George's great friend. Both had taste for painting theatrical characters, hardbake and raspberry tarts, sliding and skating in Regent's Park and Serpentine, attending plays. Rowson, Master George's appointed body-servant, conducted them to theatres, treated young master to oysters after play. Attended principal theatres of metropolis; knew names of all actors from Drury Lane to Sadler's Wells. **Mrs. Todd's private plan (rumor, not general knowledge)**: Noted Georgy and her youngest daughter Rosa Jemima "looked so well together" and privately wondered "who knows what might happen? Don't they make a pretty little couple?"

**Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury)**: Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Four boarding pupils include West Indian gentleman (no visitors) and hulking boy of three-and-twenty with neglected education. Georgy is day boy only, arrives mornings under Rowson's guardianship, rides away afternoons on pony followed by groom. Advertised system "prepared young noblemen and gentlemen for the Universities, the senate, and the learned professions" without "degrading corporal severities." Veal compliments Georgy personally on wealth and destined high station; warns him to prepare through "sedulity and docility in youth" for lofty duties; reminds him "obedience in the child was the best preparation for command in the man"; begs George not bring toffee to school. **Notable failing**: Veal frequently tolerates Georgy's late arrival and defaulting behavior without consequences. Possessed orrery, electrifying machine, turning lathe, theatre (in wash-house), chemical apparatus, "select library." Took boys to British Museum. Veal spoke "almost always," deliberately employed "very finest and longest words" of vocabulary. Weekly reports list score or more branches of knowledge with pupil's progress marked. Georgy marked: aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French, et cetera. "Everybody had prizes for everything at the end of the year."

**Amelia's Involvement with School**: Made friends with Mrs. Veal "for reasons of her own"—liked to be in house seeing Georgy come to school. Attended Mrs. Veal's monthly conversazioni with pink cards engraved with Greek goddess Athene. "Poor little Amelia never missed one of these entertainments and thought them delicious so long as she might have Georgy sitting by her." Walked from Brompton "in any weather" and embraced Mrs. Veal "with tearful gratitude for the delightful evening she had passed." **Emotional Indifference**: Georgy bears separation from Amelia easily with "a number of pleasures and consolations administered to him," whilst "his mother was yearning after him at home...every hour of the day, and during most hours of the sad lonely nights."

## Amelia's Captivity and Suffering (Chapter 24)

**Mrs. Sedley's Death and Preceding Illness**: Few months after Georgy began with paternal grandfather, Mrs. Sedley died. "There had been little love between her and the child. He did not care to show much grief. He came down to visit his mother in a fine new suit of mourning, and was very angry that he could not go to a play upon which he had set his heart." Mrs. Sedley's illness had been "the occupation and perhaps the safeguard of Amelia." Old lady never left bed; Amelia was "never absent except when she ran to see George." Old mother grudged her even those rare visits; "who had been a kind, smiling, good-natured mother once, in the days of her prosperity, but whom poverty and infirmities had broken down." Amelia bore her harshness gently; smoothed pillow; was ready with soft answer; soothed sufferer with words of hope and "closed the eyes that had once looked so tenderly upon her."

**John Sedley's Destitution**: Old man "stunned by the blow which had befallen him, and stood utterly alone in the world. His wife, his honour, his fortune, everything he loved best had fallen away from him. There was only Amelia to stand by and support with her gentle arms the tottering, heart-broken old man."

**Financial Dependence on Osborne**: "One of the many causes for personal pride with which old Osborne chose to recreate himself that Sedley, his ancient rival, enemy, and benefactor, was in his last days so utterly defeated and humiliated as to be forced to accept pecuniary obligations at the hands of the man who had most injured and insulted him." Osborne "cursed the old pauper and relieved him from time to time." As he furnished George with money for his mother, he gave boy "to understand by hints, delivered in his brutal, coarse way, that George's maternal grandfather was but a wretched old bankrupt and dependant." George carried "the pompous supplies to his mother and the shattered old widower."

**Amelia's Acceptance and Prison**: "It may have shown a want of 'proper pride' in Amelia that she chose to accept these money benefits at the hands of her father's enemy. But proper pride and this poor lady had never had much acquaintance together." Her life "had come down to this--to a mean prison and a long, ignoble bondage. Little George visited her captivity sometimes and consoled it with feeble gleams of encouragement. Russell Square was the boundary of her prison: she might walk thither occasionally, but was always back to sleep in her cell at night; to perform cheerless duties; to watch by thankless sick-beds; to suffer the harassment and tyranny of querulous disappointed old age."

**Amelia's Mourning Activities**: She determined "with all her might and strength to try and make her old father happy. She slaved, toiled, patched, and mended, sang and played backgammon, read out the newspaper, cooked dishes for old Sedley, walked him out sedulously into Kensington Gardens or the Brompton Lanes, listened to his stories with untiring smiles and affectionate hypocrisy." She sat musing by his side as old man "feeble and querulous, sunned himself on the garden benches and prattled about his wrongs or his sorrows." Sad thoughts haunted her; "The children running up and down the slopes and broad paths in the gardens reminded her of George, who was taken from her; the first George was taken from her; her selfish, guilty love, in both instances, had been rebuked and bitterly chastised. She strove to think it was right that she should be so punished. She was such a miserable wicked sinner. She was quite alone in the world." **Miniature Gift**: Georgy commissioned a miniature portrait of himself, paying from own money to create copy for his mother. Old Osborne, pleased by incident, gave boy twice the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung portrait beside another miniature over her bed. Slept with picture under pillow; kissed and wept and prayed over it "many many times." "Since her parting with George she had had no such joy and consolation."

**Burial of Mrs. Sedley**: Buried in churchyard at Brompton "upon just such a rainy, dark day as Amelia recollected when first she had been there to marry George. Her little boy sat by her side in pompous new sables." She remembered old pew-woman and clerk; thoughts were away in other times as parson read. "But that she held George's hand in her own, perhaps she would have liked to change places with...." Then "she felt ashamed of her selfish thoughts and prayed inwardly to be strengthened to do her duty."

## Major Dobbin's Return (Chapter 24)

**Illness in Madras**: Major Dobbin, having obtained leave from commandant to proceed to Madras and thence to Europe "on urgent private affairs," travelled "night and day until he reached his journey's end." Arrived at Madras "in a high fever." Servants brought him to friend's house "in a state of delirium"; thought for many days he would never travel farther than "the burying-ground of the church of St. George's, where the troops should fire a salvo over his grave."

**Delirium and Testament**: During fever, "the poor fellow lay tossing in his fever, the people who watched him might have heard him raving about Amelia. The idea that he should never see her again depressed him in his lucid hours." Made solemn preparations for departure, setting affairs in order and leaving "the little property of which he was possessed to those whom he most desired to benefit." Friend witnessed his testament. "He desired to be buried with a little brown hair-chain which he wore round his neck and which, if the truth must be known, he had got from Amelia's maid at Brussels, when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne on the plateau at Mount St. John."

**Recovery and Passage Home**: Dobbin recovered and took passage on ship Ramchunder. "Perhaps he was not inclined to put himself in his exhausted state again under the guardianship of Glorvina." Said laughingly to fellow-passenger he thought "Miss O'Dowd would have done for me...if we had had her on board."

## Jos Sedley's Return (Chapter 24)

**Ten Years in Bengal**: Jos had passed ten years in Bengal. "Constant dinners, tiffins, pale ale and claret, the prodigious labour of cutcherry, and the refreshment of brandy-pawnee which he was forced to take there, had their effect upon Waterloo Sedley." Voyage to Europe pronounced necessary. Having served full time in India with fine appointments enabling him to lay by considerable sum of money, he was free to come home with good pension or return to resume rank in service "to which his seniority and his vast talents entitled him."

**Passage on Ramchunder**: After leaving St. Helena, became "very generous, disposing of a great quantity of ship stores, claret, preserved meats, and great casks packed with soda-water, brought out for his private delectation." No ladies on board; Major gave precedency to civilian, so Jos was "the first dignitary at table, and treated by Captain Bragg and the officers of the Ramchunder with the respect which his rank warranted." Disappeared "rather in a panic during a two-days' gale" with "portholes of his cabin battened down," remained in cot reading *The Washerwoman of Finchley Common* left on board by Lady Emily Hornblower. Brought stock of novels and plays which he lent to rest of ship, "rendered himself agreeable to all by his kindness and condescension."

**Conversations with Dobbin**: "Many and many a night as the ship was cutting through the roaring dark sea, the moon and stars shining overhead and the bell singing out the watch, Mr. Sedley and the Major would sit on the quarter-deck of the vessel talking about home, as the Major smoked his cheroot and the civilian puffed at the hookah which his servant prepared for him."

## Narrative Reflection (Chapter 24)

Author reflects on Amelia's captivity: "the account of this kind of solitary imprisonment is insufferably tedious, unless there is some cheerful or humorous incident to enliven it—a tender gaoler, for instance, or a waggish commandant of the fortress...the historian has no such enlivening incident to relate in the narrative of Amelia's captivity." Emphasizes universal human experience: "So, never mind, whether she be a heroine or no; or you and I, however old, scolding, and bankrupt--may we have in our last days a kind soft shoulder on which to lean and a gentle hand to soothe our gouty old pillows."

**Philosophical Commentary**: "The hidden and awful Wisdom which apportions the destinies of mankind is pleased so to humiliate and cast down the tender, good, and wise, and to set up the selfish, the foolish, or the wicked. Oh, be humble, my brother, in your prosperity! Be gentle with those who are less lucky, if not more deserving. Think, what right have you to be scornful, whose virtue is a deficiency of temptation, whose success may be a chance, whose rank may be an ancestor's accident, whose prosperity is very likely a satire."

**Promise of Relief**: "But we are not going to leave these two people long in such a low and ungenteel station of life. Better days, as far as worldly prosperity went, were in store for both. Perhaps the ingenious reader has guessed who was the stout gentleman who called upon Georgy at his school in company with our old friend Major Dobbin. It was another old acquaintance returned to England, and at a time when his presence was likely to be of great comfort to his relatives there."
